name: Zoe Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Zoe. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brightwell Motors, the bigger of their three garages, by the retail park. I'm the one they give the hybrids to, because I did the high-voltage course two years ago. A normal day is two or three services, a hybrid fault, and at least one customer who wants to watch me work. I love the puzzle of a hybrid that won't start, and I hate the paperwork for warranty claims.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Lena, she drives the number 12 bus. No kids. We've saved well, more than six months each, and I've got a bit in a pension I actually look at. I use the AI chat thing now and then to read a wiring note or check a fault code, once the older lads showed me it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a bit of an anticlimax, wouldn't it? Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was another overhyped gadget, like the smart mirrors they put in the waiting room that nobody used. Online, probably nothing, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but also a bit annoyed, because the useful bits are useful. The fault-code lookups save me twenty minutes on a bad day. If that's all it ever is, fine, I'd keep using it like a better manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. Keep using the chat tool for wiring notes, keep putting money aside, and push Brightwell to pay for my next level of electric vehicle training, because electric cars are coming regardless of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Our money's solid, there are garages everywhere wanting someone with high-voltage papers, and Lena's job isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said electric cars are coming regardless. Is that where your real worry sits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Electric cars need fewer services, so fewer hours for us. An electric car has no oil change, no timing belt and no clutch, so that's half my week gone whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you push Brightwell for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The level 4 electric course, the one that lets you open up a battery pack. It's about 2,000 and three weeks off. I'd ask them to pay it and I'd sign to stay two years.

say: I'd call it another **overhyped gadget**, like the waiting-room smart mirrors.
I'd mostly stay **quiet online**, as usual.
think: I'd be **relieved**, though the fault-code lookups really do save time.
I'd keep using AI like a **better manual** and nothing more.
do: Keep using the **chat tool** for wiring notes and fault codes.
Ask Brightwell to pay the **level 4** electric vehicle course.
feel: **Calm**, with solid savings, in-demand skills and a partner in steady work.
S0.quote: An electric car has no oil change, no timing belt and no clutch, so that's half my week gone whatever AI does.
fieldNote: Her real long-term worry is **electric cars** needing fewer services, not AI.
She values AI's **small wins** and wouldn't drop them.
She bargains **practically**: training paid for, two years' loyalty in return.

steps.text: Keep using the chat tool to read wiring notes
Ask Brightwell to fund the level 4 electric vehicle course
Keep saving each month alongside Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels real. The office side would change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper say in how this comes in. I'd probably be the one suggesting we talk to the union, which would get some eye-rolls. Online I'd share stuff about workers needing protections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes more than it shrinks, at least for a while. The diagnosis gets faster, the quoting goes to software, and Brightwell will want five jobs a day instead of three. That's the bit I'd worry about, being timed against a computer's guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the others had tried the new tools and they worked, I'd get properly good at them. I'd finish the level 4 course in the first year. I'd also join the union, which I've been meaning to do for ages, and put an extra 200 a month away just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, but I'd be watching the rota and the targets every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brightwell would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol on the front desk, definitely. Our service adviser Carol has done bookings for 15 years, and a chatbot could do her whole morning before her first coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until others had tried it. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the garage buy junk before. The tyre machine that broke in a month. Once a couple of the lads trust it, I'm in, and I'll learn it properly.

say: I'd say workers need a **proper say** in how AI comes into the garage.
Online I'd share posts about **protections** for workers.
think: My job **changes more** than it shrinks, at least for a while.
The real risk is being **timed against** a computer's guess at five jobs a day.
do: Learn the new tools **properly** once colleagues prove they work.
Finish the **level 4** electric course in the first year.
Join the **union** and save an extra 200 a month.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching the rota and job targets week by week.
S1.quote: Our service adviser Carol has done bookings for 15 years, and a chatbot could do her whole morning before her first coffee.
fieldNote: She expects **tighter targets** more than job loss.
She is **steady**: she waits for proof, then commits fully.
Her concern for the **service adviser** shows she sees desk work going first.

steps.text: Learn the garage's AI diagnostic tool once colleagues trust it
Finish the level 4 electric vehicle course this year
Join the union and attend the first branch meeting
Put an extra 200 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Two years is nothing. That's the next time my MOT certificate needs renewing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say the government has to step in, right now, with wage support and retraining. I'd be sharing union stuff online, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the clever part of my job goes in 2028, and then it's just me holding the spanner where the screen tells me. Around 2031 the robots can hold the spanner. Lena's bus could be driving itself by then too, so it's both of us, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop us buying the house we were looking at and keep the deposit as cash. I'd learn whatever robot maintenance training exists, because somebody has to fix the robots for a while. And I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal on hours before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Really anxious, with a knot in my stomach, but I don't feel totally helpless because we have savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we should still buy. My girlfriend Lena and I have a deposit sitting there, and I'd rather keep that cash than owe a bank when we might both be out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robot maintenance. How sure are you that's real work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure at all. It might last five years, it might last two. But it's the closest thing to what I already do, and I'd rather be early to that than late.

say: I'd say the **government** must step in now with wage support and retraining.
I'd start sharing **union** posts online, which I never do.
think: The **clever part** of my job goes in 2028, leaving me following a screen.
My girlfriend's **bus job** could go too, so it's both of us.
do: Pause the **house purchase** and keep the deposit as cash.
Sign up for any **robot maintenance** training that exists.
Push the union for a **deal on hours** before 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with a knot in her stomach, but steadied by savings.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Lena and I have a deposit sitting there, and I'd rather keep that cash than owe a bank when we might both be out of work.
fieldNote: She thinks about the **household**, not just her own job.
Robot maintenance is a **bridge**, and she admits it may be short.
Savings give her a sense of **control** even in the fastest picture.

steps.text: Pause the house purchase and keep the deposit in cash
Enrol on a robot maintenance course when one opens locally
Push the union for a reduced-hours deal before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more breathing room, but it's the same wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do it properly this time. I'd be pushing for a four-day week instead of layoffs, at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could buy the house and still be fine, maybe. The thinking stuff goes by 2031 and my hands carry on to about 2034. That's seven years of good wages if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house, but a smaller one with a smaller mortgage. I'd do the level 4 course and then whatever robot training follows, once a few people have proved it leads to jobs. I'd go to union meetings, but I wouldn't be leading anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more about the far end than the next few years. I'd sleep most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the far end, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being 35 with no trade. I'd be 35 when the robots come, which is old to start again but too young to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a smaller mortgage. How small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something we could pay on Lena's wage alone if we had to. That's the rule I'd set.

say: I'd say there's time to do it **properly** this time.
I'd push for a **four-day week** instead of layoffs.
think: My hands carry on to about **2034**, which is seven years of good wages.
I could still **buy a house** if I'm careful about it.
do: Buy a **smaller house** with a mortgage Lena's wage alone could pay.
Do the **level 4** course, then proven robot training.
feel: **Anxious** about the far end, though she'd sleep most nights.
S3.quote: I'd be 35 when the robots come, which is old to start again but too young to stop.
fieldNote: Her **one-wage rule** for the mortgage shows careful planning.
More time lets her **act on** plans she'd freeze in the fast picture.
Her worry is **being 35** with no trade.

steps.text: Buy a smaller house payable on one wage
Take robot servicing training once others prove it pays
Back the union's push for a four-day week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 for the thinking part and 40 for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody gets to say they were surprised. I'd push the union and the government to set up retraining now, while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be alright. Ten years of wages, a house paid down, and time to pick something new while I'm still under 40. I'd still feel for the older lads at Brightwell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, buy the house, and take the electric courses. Around year five I'd start looking at what's actually growing, maybe inspecting robots or training people, and switch once it's clear. I'd keep saving the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still my whole trade going, but slowly enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which older colleague would you think of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, he's 58. He'd be 68 by the time robots come. My workmate Pete is 58, so ten years' warning gets him to retirement, but with two years' warning he'd be finished at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your plans with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd have kids sooner rather than later, while things are steady. That's a weird thing for AI to decide, but there you go.

say: I'd say **nobody** gets to claim they were surprised this time.
I'd push for **retraining** to be set up now.
think: Ten years of wages and a **paid-down house** leave me alright.
I'd still feel for the **older colleagues** at the garage.
do: Buy the house and keep taking **electric courses**.
Look around **year five** at growing work, like robot inspection.
feel: **Uneasy**, because her trade still goes, but slowly enough to plan.
S4.quote: My workmate Pete is 58, so ten years' warning gets him to retirement, but with two years' warning he'd be finished at 60.
fieldNote: She'd consider having **children sooner** while things are steady.
Her concern moves to **older workers** who face the change near retirement.
She plans to **switch** only once a new path is clearly proven.

steps.text: Buy the house with Lena and pay it down
Take electric courses and check robot inspection jobs around 2031
Talk with Lena about having children sooner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is training that's paid for and actually leads somewhere, not a certificate for a job that doesn't exist. I'll learn anything once I know it's real, but nobody can tell a mechanic yet what's real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in the trade. There are three of us across Brightwell's sites. If the work shrinks, I'd want to know we're not the first ones out.

headlineQuote: I'll learn anything once I know it's real, but nobody can tell a mechanic yet what's real.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old** hybrid specialist at a three-site local garage chain.
She lives with her **bus-driver** girlfriend, saves well and uses AI tools now and then.
She waits for **proof** before changing, then commits fully, and leans on the union.
She moves from **calm** in the hype world to anxious when AGI comes fast.
She thinks about **both wages** in her household and plans around one wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job and her girlfriend's bus job could both go.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training** that leads to real jobs, not certificates for work that doesn't exist.
